What Is the Web?
Meet Terra and discover how web pages are made.
Hoot hoot! I\'m Terra the owl! 🦉 Welcome to the Forest Floor, where every web page begins as a tiny seed!
Hey, I\'m Terra! Welcome to the Forest Floor — this is where you\'ll learn how web pages are built.
Every website you\'ve ever seen is made of a secret language called HTML. It tells the page what to show! 🤔
Every website is written in HTML — a markup language that describes what appears on the page: headings, text, images and more.
Look! This tiny line of HTML makes a big bold greeting appear. Soon YOU will plant words like this! 🌱
Check out this example: one h1 tag makes a big bold heading. In the next lesson you\'ll write your own.
Plant Your First Heading
Write your first HTML tag and grow a heading.
It\'s planting time! 🌱 Today you write your very first HTML all by yourself. I\'m so excited!
Time to write your first HTML for real. It\'s easier than you think — one tag, one word.
In this lesson you will write your first HTML element: a level-one heading.
HTML tags are like little flower pots. The h1 pot holds the BIGGEST words on the page! 🪴
An h1 tag marks the most important heading on a page. Whatever you put between the opening and closing tag shows up big and bold.
The h1 element defines the top-level heading. Content placed between the opening and closing tags is rendered as the page title.
See how the word Sprout sits inside the tags? That\'s how we plant a word-seed! 🌱
Here\'s the pattern: the word Sprout goes between the opening h1 tag and the closing one.
Note the structure: opening tag, text content, closing tag. You will reproduce this in the editor.
Now it\'s your turn! Plant the word Sprout in the playground and watch it grow! You can do it! 💪
Your turn — open the playground and write the heading yourself. I\'ll be right here if you need a hint.
Complete the challenge in the editor. A hint is available if needed.
Write the word Sprout inside the h1 tags so it appears as a big heading.
Type Sprout between the opening h1 tag and the closing h1 tag — the pots are already there!
Page Skeleton
Arrange the bones of a full HTML page.
Every web page has a skeleton, just like every tree has a trunk and branches! 🌳
Every proper web page follows the same skeleton: a doctype, an html element, a head and a body.
Look at the shape! DOCTYPE comes first, then html wraps around the head and the body. 🦴
Here\'s the structure: DOCTYPE first, then html wrapping head (page info) and body (what you see).
Now let\'s build it! Drag the blocks into the right order and the skeleton will stand up! 🧩
Your turn: put the blocks in the right order to build a complete page skeleton.
Arrange the blocks to build a complete HTML page: DOCTYPE first, then html, head, body and the closing tags.
DOCTYPE always comes first. The head goes before the body, and closing tags mirror the opening ones.
Headings and Paragraphs
Mix big headings with flowing paragraph text.
A page with only headings would SHOUT all the time! 📣 We need calm paragraph text too.
Headings grab attention, but paragraphs carry the real story. Pages need both.
The h2 tag makes a medium heading, and the p tag holds a sentence. Look how nicely they sit together! 🪺
Use h2 for section headings and p for paragraphs. Here\'s an example with both.
Your turn! Write a heading about something you love, then tell me about it in a paragraph! ✏️
Now write your own: one h2 heading and one p paragraph about anything you like.
Write an h2 heading and a p paragraph below it about any topic you like.
You need two tags: h2 for the heading and p for the paragraph. Don\'t forget the closing tags!
Links and Images
Connect pages with links and show pictures.
Links are like magic bridges between pages, and images are pictures we pin to our page! 🌉🖼️
Links connect pages together — that\'s what makes the web a web. Images bring pages to life.
The a tag makes a clickable link with href, and the img tag shows a picture with src. Look! 👀
The a tag needs an href attribute for the destination. The img tag needs src for the picture and alt to describe it.
Now build your own bridge and pin your own picture! You\'re becoming a real web wanderer! 🧭
Your turn: add one link and one image to the page. Earn that Web Wanderer badge!
Add one link using the a tag and one picture using the img tag.
The a tag needs href=\"...\" and the img tag needs src=\"...\". Copy the pattern from the example.
Making Lists
Collect things in tidy bullet-point lists.
Time to collect treasures! 🍄 Lists keep all your favorite things in a neat row of bullet points.
Lists are everywhere on the web — menus, to-dos, rankings. Let\'s learn the tags behind them.
The ul tag is the basket, and each li tag is one treasure inside it! See the fern and mushroom? 🧺
A ul tag wraps the whole list, and each item lives in its own li tag. Like this example.
Make a bullet list with a ul tag holding three li items — things you found in the forest.
Open with ul, then add one li tag for each item, then close the ul. Each li needs a closing tag too.
Your First CSS
Paint your HTML with a splash of color.
HTML plants the garden, but CSS paints it! 🎨 Today we give your words beautiful colors!
HTML is structure, CSS is style. Time to add some color to your pages.
Look! This little spell tells every h1 to turn green, like a fresh leaf! 🍃
A CSS rule picks a tag (like h1) and sets properties — here, color: green makes the heading green.
Now you try! Pick any color you like and paint your heading inside the style tags! 🖌️
Your turn: write a CSS rule inside the style tags that gives the heading a color of your choice.
Inside the style tags, write a CSS rule that gives the h1 heading a color.
Write h1 { color: green; } inside the style tags — or pick any color you like!
Colors and Layout
Style the whole page: background and centering.
Let\'s paint the WHOLE page this time! 🌈 A background color makes everything feel cozy.
You can style the entire page by targeting the body — background colors, alignment and more.
See? background-color paints the page, and text-align: center moves everything to the middle! ✨
Two properties to remember: background-color sets the page color, and text-align: center centers the text.
Give the body a background color and center the text with text-align: center.
Inside the body rule add background-color: with any color, and text-align: center on a second line.
Mini Page Project
Build a complete little web page on your own.
This is it — your first WHOLE page! 🎉 Everything you\'ve learned comes together today!
Final challenge of the Forest Floor: build a complete page using everything you\'ve learned.
You\'ll need a big h1 heading, a paragraph, and a list with items. You know all of these! 🧠
The page needs an h1 heading, a p paragraph, and a ul list with li items. You\'ve used all of them before.
I believe in you, little builder! Finish this page and you\'ll be a true HTML Hero! 🦸
Finish this and the HTML Hero badge is yours. Take your time and build something you like.
Inside the body, build a page with an h1 heading, a p paragraph, and a ul list with li items.
Add them one at a time: first h1, then p, then a ul with at least one li inside.
Hello, print()!
Make Python speak with your first print().
Welcome to the Sunny Meadow! 🌻 Here we speak Python — and the first word is print()!
Welcome to Python! The first thing every coder learns is print() — it makes the program talk.
Look! print() shouts whatever you put inside the quotes. This one says hello to the meadow! 📣
print() outputs whatever text you put between the quotes. Here it prints a greeting.
Your turn, little coder! Make Python say Hello, meadow! out loud! 🌼
Now you try it — write a print() that greets the meadow.
Use print() to output the message Hello, meadow!
Write print(\"Hello, meadow!\") — don\'t forget the quotes and parentheses.
Variables
Store values in labelled jars called variables.
Variables are like labelled jars! 🫙 We can keep a name in one jar and a number in another.
Variables store values under a name so you can reuse them — text, numbers, anything.
See the jars? plant_name holds Sunflower and plant_age holds 3. The f before the quotes mixes them into a sentence! 🌻
Here plant_name and plant_age hold values, and the f-string puts them inside a sentence using curly braces.
Now you print a sentence using BOTH jars! Tell me about the sunflower! 💬
Your turn: print one sentence that uses both variables.
Print a sentence that uses both plant_name and plant_age, so the output shows Sunflower and 3.
Try an f-string: print(f\"{plant_name} is {plant_age} years old\") — the braces drop the values in.
Strings and Numbers
Add numbers together and make words shout.
Numbers and words are different creatures! 🤔 Numbers can add up, and words can do tricks like SHOUTING!
Python treats numbers and strings differently. Numbers do math; strings have handy methods like .upper().
Look! 4 + 3 seeds makes 7, and word.upper() turns meadow into MEADOW! Magic! ✨
Adding numbers gives a total, and .upper() returns the string in uppercase. Both get printed here.
Print the seed total (it should be 7), then print the word in UPPERCASE using .upper().
print(seeds) shows the total, and print(word.upper()) shouts MEADOW.
Asking with input()
Let your program ask questions and listen.
Until now your code only talked. Today it LISTENS too! 👂 input() lets the user type something!
Programs get interesting when they listen. input() pauses and waits for the user to type something.
See? input() catches what the user types and keeps it in the name jar. Then we greet them! 👋
input() returns whatever was typed, and we store it in a variable. Then an f-string builds the greeting.
Try it! Ask for a name and say a big friendly hello to whoever answers! 😊
Your turn: read a name with input() and print a greeting that includes it.
Read a name with input() and print a friendly greeting that includes that name.
The name is already in the name variable — print it with an f-string like print(f\"Hello, {name}!\").
If and Else
Teach your code to make decisions.
Hmm, should I fly or nap? 🤔 Code makes choices too — with if and else!
Programs make decisions with if and else: if a condition is true, do one thing; otherwise, do another.
Look! If the sun level is bigger than 5, we say Sunny day! Otherwise we say Cloudy day. ☀️☁️
The condition sun_level > 5 is checked first. True runs the if branch, false runs the else branch. Mind the indentation!
Now you be the weather owl! Check the sun level and announce the day! 🦉
Your turn: write the weather check yourself. The sun level is 8, so guess which message will print.
If sun_level is more than 5, print Sunny day! — otherwise print Cloudy day.
Start with if sun_level > 5: then an indented print. Add else: with its own indented print below.
For Loops
Repeat actions without repeating yourself.
Five butterflies are visiting! 🦋 Should we write five prints? No way — a loop does it for us!
When you need to repeat something, don\'t copy-paste — use a for loop with range().
Look! for i in range(5) runs the print five times, counting each butterfly one by one! 🔁
range(5) gives 0 to 4, and the loop body runs once for each. i + 1 makes the count start at 1.
Now greet all five butterflies with your own loop! They\'re waiting for you! 🦋🦋🦋
Your turn: write a loop that greets each of the five butterflies.
Use a for loop with range to greet each of the five butterflies.
Write for i in range(5): then an indented print that mentions Butterfly — try an f-string with i + 1.
Lists
Keep many things in one seed pouch.
A list is like a seed pouch — it holds lots of things in one place! 🌰 Let\'s peek inside!
Lists hold many values in one variable. You can add to them, count them and loop over them.
See? append() drops a new seed into the pouch, and len() counts how many seeds we have! 🔢
.append() adds an item to the end of the list, and len() tells you how many items it holds.
Now add a lotus seed to your pouch, then show me the pouch and count the seeds! 🪷
Your turn: append \"lotus\", then print the list and its length.
Add the word lotus to the seeds list with append, then print the list and how many seeds it holds.
Use seeds.append(\"lotus\"), then print(seeds) and print(len(seeds)) — the count should be 4.
Functions
Build a reusable greeting machine with def.
Imagine a magic machine: put a name in, and a greeting pops out! 🎰 That\'s a function!
Functions are reusable blocks of code. Define them once with def, then call them as many times as you like.
Look! def greet(name) builds the machine, and greet(\"Terra\") makes it say Namaste, Terra! 🙏
def greet(name): defines the function with a parameter. Calling greet(\"Terra\") runs the body with that name.
Now fix the machine so it says Namaste to everyone! Terra and Asha are waiting! 😊
Your turn: make the greet function print a Namaste greeting for whichever name it receives.
Change the greet function so it prints Namaste, followed by the name it was given.
Inside greet, replace the print with print(f\"Namaste, {name}!\") so each call greets the right person.
Bug Hunt
Rebuild a scrambled watering program.
Oh no! 🐞 My watering program fell apart and all the lines got scrambled! The plants are thirsty!
Uh oh — this watering script got scrambled. The lines are all there, just in the wrong order.
Let\'s think like detectives! 🔍 First we need the plant list, then the counter, THEN the loop that waters each one.
Think about the flow: set up the list and counter first, then loop through the plants, then report the total.
You can do this! Put the blocks back in order and save the thirsty plants! 💧
Reorder the blocks so the program waters every plant and counts them correctly.
Arrange the blocks so the program waters every plant in the list and then reports how many were watered.
Create the list and set watered to 0 first. The two indented lines belong inside the for loop. The final print comes last.
Guess the Number
Build a tiny guessing game with if, elif, else.
Game time! 🎲 I\'m thinking of a secret number, and your code will tell players if they guessed right!
Let\'s build an actual game: the player guesses a number and your code says if it\'s too low, too high or correct.
Look at the three roads: too low, too high, or correct! if, elif and else pick the right one! 🛤️
Three branches: if for too low, elif for too high, else for the correct guess. One of them always runs.
You\'ve learned so much, little coder! Build the game and let\'s play together! 🥳
Last lesson of the meadow — build the comparison and finish your first game. Nice work getting here!
Compare guess with secret: print Too low!, Too high!, or Correct! depending on the guess.
Use if guess < secret: for Too low!, elif guess > secret: for Too high!, and else: for Correct!
Card Layouts
Shape content into soft, rounded cards with CSS.
Welcome to the River Delta! 🌊 Here we shape our pages like smooth river stones — round and cozy!
Welcome to the River Delta. Real websites organize content into cards — let\'s learn how.
Three spells make a card: padding gives space inside, border-radius rounds the corners, and a background color paints it! 🎨
A card needs three CSS properties: padding for inner space, border-radius for rounded corners, and a background color.
Now shape your own river-stone card! Make it smooth and colorful! 🪨
Your turn: style the card class with all three properties.
Style the card with padding, border-radius, and a background color.
Inside .card add three lines: padding: 16px; border-radius: 12px; and background-color: with any color.
Forms
Build a form that asks visitors questions.
How do websites ask questions? 🤔 With forms! Boxes to type in and buttons to press!
Forms are how websites collect input — search bars, sign-ups, surveys. They\'re all forms.
A form has a label that explains, an input box to type in, and a button to send. Look at them work together! 📨
Inside a form tag you need a label to describe the field, an input for typing, and a button to submit.
Now build a river survey! Ask the fish what they think! 🐟
Your turn: complete the river survey form with all three pieces.
Inside the form, add a label, a text input, and a button.
You need three tags inside the form: label with some text, input with type=\"text\", and button with a caption.
Page Sections
Organize a page with header, main and footer.
Big pages need neighborhoods! 🏘️ A header at the top, a main in the middle, and a footer at the bottom!
Real pages are organized into semantic sections: header, nav, main and footer. It keeps everything tidy.
Let\'s build the Delta Diary page! Drag the sections into place from top to bottom! 🧩
Arrange the blocks: header first, then nav, then main with its section inside, and footer last.
Arrange the blocks to build the Delta Diary page: header, nav, main with a section inside, then footer.
Top to bottom: header, nav, main. The section block sits inside main, and footer always comes last.
Profile Card Project
Build and style your own profile card.
Project time! 🎉 Let\'s build a profile card all about YOU — with a picture, your name and your story!
Mini project: a profile card like the ones on real social sites — image, name, bio, styled with CSS.
You\'ll need an img for the picture, an h2 for your name, a p for your story, and round corners to make it pretty! 🖼️
The card needs an img, an h2 with your name, a p with a short bio, and border-radius in the CSS.
Finish this card and you\'ll earn the River Builder badge! I\'m so proud of you! 🏗️
Finish the card and the River Builder badge is yours. Make it look good!
Build a profile card with an image, an h2 name, a bio paragraph, and rounded corners using border-radius.
Add img, h2 and p inside the profile div, then set border-radius in the .profile CSS rule.
Even or Odd
Sort numbers into even and odd with logic.
Welcome to the Deep Grove! 🌳 Here numbers hide secrets — some are even, some are odd. Can we sort them?
Welcome to the Deep Grove. First challenge: classify numbers as even or odd using the modulo operator.
The modulo sign tells us the leftover after dividing! If n mod 2 leaves nothing, the number is even! 🔢
The modulo operator gives the remainder after dividing by 2. If it equals 0, the number is even — otherwise odd.
Arrange the blocks so the program checks each number and prints whether it is even or odd.
The list comes first, then the for loop. Inside it: the if check, its print, then else with its print.
Working with Data
Sort and sum a list of snack prices.
The trail snack stand has prices everywhere! 🍪 Let\'s tidy them up and find the cheapest treat!
Real programs crunch data all the time. Let\'s sort a list of prices and pull useful facts out of it.
Watch! sort() lines the prices up from small to big, prices[0] grabs the cheapest, and sum() adds them ALL up! 🧮
.sort() orders the list, prices[0] is then the smallest value, and sum(prices) totals everything.
Sort the prices, then print the cheapest price and the total of all prices.
Call prices.sort() first, then print(prices[0]) for the cheapest (30) and print(sum(prices)) for the total (280).
Reusable Functions
Write one function and use it for every garden bed.
We have lots of garden beds to measure! 🌷 Instead of doing the math again and again, let\'s build ONE helper!
When you repeat the same calculation, wrap it in a function with parameters — write once, use everywhere.
See? rectangle_area takes a width and a height, multiplies them, and announces the area! 📐
rectangle_area takes two parameters and prints width * height. Each call can pass different numbers.
Now fix the function and measure the 4 by 5 bed and the 3 by 3 bed! The flowers are counting on you! 🌸
Your turn: make the function print the real area, then call it for a 4 x 5 bed and a 3 x 3 bed.
Make rectangle_area print the real area, then call it for a 4 x 5 bed and a 3 x 3 bed.
Print width * height inside the function, then call rectangle_area(4, 5) and rectangle_area(3, 3) — expect 20 and 9.
Vowel Counter
Solve a real puzzle: count the vowels in a word.
Challenge time! 🧠 The word himalaya is hiding vowels — a, e, i, o, u. Can your code find them all?
Time for a proper problem: count how many vowels appear in the word himalaya. No step-by-step recipe this time.
Here\'s my secret plan: look at each letter one by one, and if it\'s a vowel, add one to a counter! 🕵️
Think it through: loop over each letter, check if it\'s in \"aeiou\", and bump a counter when it is.
You have all the tools: a loop, an if, and a counter. Go find those vowels — I believe in you! 💪
You\'ve got loops, conditions and counters. Combine them and print the total. Good luck!
Count how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) appear in the word and print the total.
Loop with for letter in word: and check if letter in \"aeiou\": to add 1 to a counter. himalaya has 4 vowels.
Mountain Lodge Page
A three-step web project: structure, content, style.
Welcome to the Mountain Peaks! 🏔️ Our big mission: build a whole page for a cozy mountain lodge, step by step!
Welcome to the Mountain Peaks. This is a real multi-step project: a complete page for a mountain lodge.
This project covers a full page build in three steps: header content, a structured trail section, and page styling.
Three steps to the top: 1) the lodge name in a big heading, 2) a list of three trails, 3) paint it with style! 🥾
Step 1: lodge name in an h1 plus a tagline. Step 2: a section with an h2 and a ul of three trails. Step 3: CSS styling.
Follow the signs in the starter code — the comments show exactly where each step goes. Climb on! 🧗
The starter code has comments marking each step. Work through them in order — you know every tag involved.
Complete all 3 steps: add the lodge h1 and tagline, a section with an h2 and a ul of three trails, then style the page with a background color and font-family.
Work step by step: h1 in the header, h2 plus ul with li items in main, then background-color and font-family in the style block.
Trail Report Generator
Write a clean Python script with functions and loops.
Time for clean code, little ranger! 🧹 We\'ll write a trail report that\'s tidy, neat and easy to read!
Pro coders care about clean code: small functions, clear names, no repetition. Let\'s build a trail report that way.
This project emphasizes clean structure: a small focused function, a loop over parallel lists, and a summary line.
Look at describe_trail — one tiny machine that prints one tidy line for any trail! We\'ll use it for all three! 🛤️
describe_trail(name, km) prints one formatted line. Define it once, then call it inside a loop for each trail.
Three steps: build the machine, loop through the trails, then add up all the kilometres. You\'ve got this! ⛰️
Plan: write the function, loop through the trails calling it, then print the total distance. Step by step.
Write describe_trail(name, km), loop through the trails to describe each one, then print the total distance.
Use range(len(trail_names)) or zip to pair names with kms, call describe_trail for each, then print(sum(trail_kms)) — the total is 26.
Lander Rescue
Fix a while loop and land the mountain lander safely.
Mayday! 🛬 The mountain lander\'s landing code is broken — and some sneaky wrong blocks got mixed in!
Debug mission: the lander\'s countdown loop is scrambled, and a couple of trap blocks were mixed in.
Think hard! 🤔 The fuel must go DOWN each time, or the loop never ends and we circle forever!
Watch out for infinite loops: the condition must be fuel > 0, and fuel has to decrease inside the loop.
Pick only the right blocks, line them up, and bring our lander home! 🛰️
Skip the distractor blocks, order the real ones, and land safely.
Arrange the correct blocks so the lander counts its fuel down from 5 and touches down safely. Watch out for trap blocks!
Start with fuel = 5 and while fuel > 0:. Inside the loop, print the fuel and subtract 1. Avoid blocks that add fuel or check fuel < 0.
Find the Tallest Peak
Write your own algorithm to find the biggest number.
See all those peaks? 🏔️ We\'ll find the TALLEST one ourselves — no shortcuts, just brain power!
Algorithms are step-by-step recipes. Today: find the largest number in a list without using max().
This lesson covers a classic linear scan: track the current maximum while iterating through a list, without built-in helpers.
Here\'s the trick: remember the tallest peak so far, and every time we see a taller one, swap it in! 🔁
Start with the first peak as tallest. For each peak, if it\'s bigger than tallest, update tallest. Simple but powerful.
Now soar like an eagle and find that giant peak! Print its height when you spot it! 🦅
Your turn: write the loop, keep tallest up to date, and print the answer at the end.
Loop through the peaks, keep tallest updated when you find a bigger one, then print the tallest height. No max() allowed!
Inside the for loop, write if p > tallest: then tallest = p. Print tallest after the loop — it should be 8848.
What Is an API?
Learn how programs talk to each other.
Welcome above the clouds! ☁️ Up here, programs send little letters to each other — that\'s what an API is!
Welcome to the Sky Canopy. Time for a big idea: APIs — the way programs talk to other programs.
This concept lesson introduces APIs: structured interfaces that let one program request data or services from another.
Imagine a restaurant! 🍽️ You ask the waiter for momo, and the kitchen sends it back. The waiter is the API!
Think of a restaurant: you give an order (request), the kitchen prepares it, the waiter brings it back (response). The API is the waiter.
An API defines a contract: a client sends a structured request, the server processes it and returns a structured response.
Look! An app asks the sky: how\'s the weather in Pokhara? And the answer comes back: clear and 21 degrees! 🌤️
Here\'s a real example: a GET request asks for Pokhara\'s weather, and the response comes back as structured data with sky and temp.
One day your apps will ask the whole world questions like this! Isn\'t that amazing? 🌍
Weather apps, games, chat — they all run on APIs. When you build connected apps later, this is the foundation.
Paint the Sky
Creative coding: design your own sky with CSS clouds.
Art time! 🎨 Today we paint a whole sky with code — and float fluffy clouds across it!
Creative coding session: design a sky scene using only divs and CSS. You\'re the artist here.
A cloud is just a div wearing a costume: a soft color and SUPER round corners! Make at least two! ☁️☁️
Each cloud is a div with a background color and a large border-radius. The sky div gets its own background too.
Paint it YOUR way — sunset orange, night blue, anything! There\'s no wrong sky! 🌅
Make it yours — any colors, any mood. As long as the sky has a title and at least two clouds, it counts.
Build a sky scene: give the sky a background color, shape soft clouds with border-radius, and add an h1 title with at least two cloud divs.
Set background-color on .sky and .cloud, add border-radius to .cloud, then put an h1 and two divs with class cloud inside the sky.
Ecosystem Capstone
The final challenge: a full ecosystem health report.
This is it, little coder — the FINAL challenge! 🌈 Write a health report for our whole ecosystem!
The capstone. Everything you\'ve learned — functions, loops, conditions — goes into one ecosystem health report.
The capstone combines functions, iteration and branching: classify each species count and produce a summary report.
The plan: a health checker that says thriving, stable or needs care — then check every species and count everyone! 📋
